newsitem.title: USA: Maine nun killer insane, not guilty of murder.
newsitem.headline: Maine nun killer insane, not guilty of murder.

text.p: A man who admitted killing two elderly nuns in a bloody rampage through their Catholic convent was found not guilty of murder Wednesday by reason of insanity.

Somerset County Superior Court Judge Donald Alexander issued the verdict after a week and a half-long trial that focused on whether Mark Bechard, who had a history of mental illness, knew what he was doing when he killed the nuns.

Bechard, 38, was arrested on Jan. 27 inside the Servants of the Blessed Sacrament convent in Waterville while the attack was under way. He admitted to police he had killed the nuns, with whom he regularly attended mass.

Alexander, who heard the case without a jury, ruled that Bechard could not be held criminally responsible for his actions because he was too ill with delusions at the time of the attack to realize what he was doing was wrong.
Bechard had been charged with two counts of murder and two counts of attempted murder. Alexander ordered him committed to the custody of state mental health officials.
He could be freed if doctors ever determine he is cured but experts who testified during the trial said they expected him to remain institutionalized for life.

"I don't think there is any reasonable expectation of (his release) happening," his attorney Michaela Murphey said. Bechard showed no emotion when the verdict was read, according to reporters in the courtroom.
Two nuns were also seriously injured in the attack, while five others hid to escape harm. The convent, which is run by a small Cathlic church order, has remained open.
"There are no winners and we know that," Provincial Mother Superior Josephine Roney told reporters outside the sisters' chapel in Waterville, adding that they felt the justice system had worked well.
"We pray for ourselves, yes, but we pray for our city, our state and for everyone who needs healing. And we pray for Mark Bechard himself," she said.

According to trial testimony, Bechard had been asked to leave an evening mass because he was disruptive. He returned to the convent 20 minutes later and became enraged when the terrified nuns tried to keep him outside.

Police reported a horrific scene when they arrived. Bechard was beating a victim with a Virgin Mary statue, one nun had a knife in her face and another had been beaten with her own metal cane until it broke.
Bechard had been briefly institutionalized in 1994 and 1995. The murders prompted state authorities to review why he was released but no evidence of wrongdoing was found.
